title: runtime-fault-tolerance-and-fallback-spec
body:
Purpose

This document captures proposed runtime fault tolerance and fallback behaviors for the serving runtime: OOM recovery, retry semantics, and circuit breakers. It focuses on how these behaviors interact with kernel selection, scheduler policies, and the KV cache. The goal is to define deterministic, observable, and testable mechanisms for keeping customer inference online while minimizing cost and preserving output correctness.

Scope and goals
- Survive transient and saturating failures of GPUs and host memory without cascading application errors.
- Provide fast, predictable fallback paths (model variant, quantized variant, different hardware tier) when primary execution path fails.
- Minimize duplicated work and token re-generation across retries and fallbacks.
- Offer clear metrics and traces to debug failures and verify SLAs.
- Integrate with scheduling (batching) and KV cache to avoid cache poisoning or incorrect reuse.

Non-goals
- Full redesign of scheduler or kernel selection; this doc extends existing components.
- Replacing hardware-level drivers or vendor OOM mitigations.

Failure modes we consider
1) Device OOM at inference time for a batch or single large sequence.
2) Host OOM when assembling inputs or during pre/post-processing.
3) GPU timeout / driver reset leading to transient unavailability.
4) Per-request library errors (cuBLAS, custom fused kernels) returning non-deterministic failures.
5) Persistent hardware fault (GPU permanently offline).
6) Network interruption between control-plane and worker causing RPC failures.

Principles and constraints
- Fail fast and fail safe: prefer returning a controlled error or graceful fallback over hanging requests.
- Preserve determinism where possible: avoid returning partially computed tokens.
- Prefer cheap fallbacks first (retry, smaller batch, faster kernel) before expensive ones (model downgrade, cross-region).
- Make all fallbacks visible in telemetry and per-request traces.
- Avoid invalidating or reusing stale KV cache entries during recovery.

High-level behaviors
1) OOM detection and classification
   - Worker runtime must detect memory allocation failures (CUDA OOM, CPU allocation failure) and classify by scope: per-request, per-batch, per-worker.
   - For GPU OOMs, capture diagnostics: attempted allocation size, current available GPU memory, active batch size, sequence lengths, kernel used, model variant, and quantization level.

2) Local recovery attempt (fast path)
   - If OOM occurs during a batch, immediately rollback any partial token outputs and mark the affected requests as "in-retry" with a small backoff window (configurable, default 50-200ms).
   - Attempt in-order recovery strategies in this preference order: 1) reduce batch size (split into smaller sub-batches preserving KV cache prefix alignment), 2) switch to a lower-memory kernel implementation, 3) switch to quantized model variant (if available and quality budget permits).
   - Each recovery at this stage must be attempted on the same worker if worker remains healthy to preserve warm KV cache locality. If kernel/variant swap is used, annotate request trace and telemetry.

3) Scheduler-aware retries
   - Scheduler must support transactional batch split: original batch ID retained, sub-batch IDs created; requests keep original ordering guarantees for single-request semantics.
   - When splitting a batch, ensure KV cache alignment: only split on prefix boundaries, or materialize a safe prefix snapshot so subsequent generation keeps consistency. Splitting mid-KV-prefix is disallowed.
   - Retry attempts should be limited (configurable default max_retries=2 for fast local retries). Retries must be idempotent from the client-visible viewpoint (no duplicate tokens).

4) Circuit breakers and graded fallback policies
   - Per-worker circuit breaker: track recent failure rate (sliding window 1m) and average latency/error. If error rate > threshold (default 5%) or repeated OOMs within window, open circuit to route new requests away from worker for a cooldown period.
   - Per-model-variant circuit breaker: if a specific kernel or quantization variant exhibits a high error rate, temporarily mark it unhealthy in model catalog routing.
   - Global emergency fallback: when capacity is globally constrained or many workers are unhealthy, automatically route to pre-configured fallback variants (e.g., smaller model, lower seq_len cap) per customer policy. This must be a last resort and requires rate-limiting to avoid wholesale quality collapse.

5) Cross-worker fallback and warmup
   - If local retries fail or worker becomes unhealthy, the scheduler tries cross-worker fallback: reroute to a compatible worker (prefer same region, then same tier).
   - To avoid cold-start overheads and long latency, maintain a small pool of warm workers or pre-warmed quantized variants (configurable per deployment).

6) KV cache consistency during recovery
   - KV cache entries must be versioned and tagged with executing worker and model-variant. During a retry on a different kernel/worker/variant, runtime must decide whether to reuse cached KV or re-compute prefix: rules: 1) if crossing quantization boundary (FP16 -> int8), do not reuse KV; 2) if switching kernels but staying on same model-variant and precision, reuse KV only if kernel author guarantees identical KV layout; 3) if routing to different worker but same model, reuse KV only if cache sync exists (rare). Otherwise, re-compute prefix to guarantee correctness.
   - Record diagnostic flags when KV reuse is skipped for transparency.

7) Retry semantics and client-visible behavior
   - By default, retries are transparent to clients: either a successful response or a well-formed error (with failure_reason enum). We do not attempt to return partially generated tokens.
   - For streaming responses, if a retry is required after partial stream emitted, runtime must emit a streaming error event and, if configured by customer, attempt a re-issue of the entire response via non-streaming or a new stream with a new request id. Clients must be prepared to handle an 'incomplete_stream' closure code.

8) Observability and debugging signals
   - Per-request fields to include in traces/metrics: fallback_taken (bool), fallback_reason (string), fallback_path (e.g., split_batch->kernel_swap->quantized), original_worker, final_worker, kv_reused (bool), retry_count, failure_class (OOM/Driver/Timeout).
   - Aggregate metrics: per-worker OOM rate, per-kernel failure rate, per-model-variant circuit-open count, average retry count, percent of requests hitting fallback, tail latency added by fallback.
   - Export raw GPU diagnostics on OOMs for periodic analysis.

9) Backpressure and admission control
   - If the system detects sustained OOMs due to high concurrency, the admission controller should apply backpressure: temporarily reduce allowed batch sizes, reject new low-priority requests with informative error recommending retry-after, or queue requests with TTL.

10) Safety and customer controls
   - Expose per-customer policies: fallback_allowed (bool), max_quality_degradation (enum: none/minor/major), preferred_fallbacks (list: quantized, smaller-model, cross-region), retry_policy (max_retries, backoff_ms).
   - For enterprise customers that require deterministic output, allow disabling retries and fallbacks (fail-fast), with explicit SLA implications documented.

11) Testing and verification
   - Fault-injection harness: simulate GPU OOM, host OOM, driver resets, and kernel errors in staging and CI. Verify no token duplication and KV consistency.
   - Load tests that ramp concurrency and teach thresholds for circuit breakers and admission control.
   - Chaos tests for cross-worker reroutes ensuring trace continuity.

Implementation notes and interactions
- Kernels: each kernel must advertise memory profile and KV layout compatibility. The kernel registry will include fields: memory_overhead_estimate, kv_layout_id, supported_precisions. The scheduler uses memory profile to pre-emptively avoid dangerous combinations for large sequences.
- Scheduler: expose a transactional batch transformation API to split/retry without losing request context. Scheduler must co-ordinate with runtime on safe split points w.r.t. KV.
- KV cache: add version tags and explicit compatibility checks. When warming fallback workers, optionally materialize KV snapshots for hot prefixes (costly but useful for enterprise low-latency).

Operational playbook (summary)
- Detecting high OOM rate: SRE alerts if per-worker OOM rate > 0.5% sustained per hour.
- Auto-mitigation: open worker circuit, reduce batch caps, spin warm workers.
- Postmortem checklist: collect traces, GPU allocation logs, kernel selection logs, and KV cache compatibility flags.

Open questions
- How aggressive should kernel swapping be vs. batch splitting for very latency-sensitive requests?
- Do we want to support client-visible 'retry hints' so SDKs can adapt behavior?
- Cost model for maintaining warm quantized pools vs. the benefit in reduced fallbacks — what thresholds make sense per customer?

Appendix: short examples
1) Single-request OOM while using fused attention kernel: runtime detects OOM -> rollback -> attempt kernel_swap to non-fused (lower peak mem) -> success. Log: fallback_path=[kernel_swap], kv_reused=false.
2) Large batch OOM at tail generation: attempt split into 2 sub-batches preserving KV boundaries -> first sub-batch succeeds (with same worker), second sub-batch triggers persistent OOM -> route second sub-batch to fallback worker with quantized variant -> success; client receives combined response with no duplicate tokens.

Next steps
- Iterate on kernel registry schema (kv_layout_id semantics).
- Prototype batch-split transactional API in scheduler (Spike, 2w).
- Add KV tagging and compatibility checks in cache subsystem (Spike, 2w).
- Implement per-worker circuit breaker and integrate with routing decisions (3w).
- Build fault-injection tests and include in CI.
